To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the elastic modulus of enamel decreases from the nano- (E(nano)) to the meso-scale (Emeso) by about two orders of magnitude (E(nano) = 110 GPa, Emeso = 0.8 GPa), and that the flexural strength of the same material decreases from about 1.2 to 0.2 GPa.
enamel exhibits a transition from a linear elastic to a damage-tolerant material behaviour when moving from the nano- (bulk) towards the mesoscale (microstructure).

(i) the flexural strength of dental enamel decreases with increasing hierarchical level, (ii) the elastic modulus decreases with increasing hierarchical levels, (iii) the elastic modulus of enamel decreases with increasing damage tolerance and (iv) the transition from brittle to elastic-inelastic behaviour occurs at the level of the enamel rod.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a quantitative analysis of the mechanical properties of a biological, hierarchical material, which provides a deeper understanding of the mechanical performance of such materials and is a step towards the development of synthetic hierarchical structures.
the mechanical performance and the transition of the flexural strength and the elastic modulus of a hierarchically structured biological material.
the hierarchical mechanical performance of a biological composite and its implications for biomimetic materials design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transition in mechanical behaviour is a result of a change from a brittle to a damage-tolerant regime.
enamel is a damage-tolerant material, which can sustain high stresses and deformations, but only up to a certain level.

the hierarchical structure of dental enamel is optimized to be hard and stiff, but also damage-tolerant, which can be explained by a transition in mechanical properties from brittle to damage tolerant with increasing dimension of hierarchy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hierarchical structure of enamel leads to a transition from brittle to a damage-tolerant mechanical behaviour.
the mechanical properties of enamel decrease with decreasing dimension, and the transition from brittle to ductile behaviour is observed at the micro-scale.
, for the first time, we were able to determine and analyse flexural strength and modulus at three hierarchical levels of dental enamel.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transition from brittle to elastic-inelastic behaviour occurs at a hierarchical dimension of approximately 100 nm.
the mechanical behaviour of hierarchical structures is determined by the interaction between the different levels of hierarchy.
the mechanical properties of biological materials depend strongly on the level of hierarchy and are not additive.
